newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Phone co Rostelekom future unclear.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Phone co Rostelekom future unclear.

text.p: Plans to transfer a stake in Russian national phone company Rostelekom to the Svyazinvest state telecoms holding could help modernise the industry but the outlook for the companies is uncertain, analysts said on Friday.

Shares in Rostelekom, among Russia's most actively traded, rose after the State Property Committee said there were no plans to convert them into stock in the new company. But analysts said Svyazinvest's aims were unclear.

"Fundamentally Rostelekom remains the same company. The question is whether the management of Svyazinvest will try to play a big role in running Rostelekom or not," Renaissance Capital telecoms analyst Yuri Krapivin said.

Property committee spokesman Igor Plotnikov told Reuters the entire 38 percent state stake in Rostelekom would be transferred to Svyazinvest, a company founded last year to hold the state's shares in 85 regional telecom companies.
A stake in the newly-formed company would then be offered to portfolio investors, rather than to a single strategic investor.
"Rostelekom will remain an independent company, but in practice will become a subsidiary of the holding company," Plotnikov said.

Par Mellstroem, telecoms analyst at Brunswick Brokerage, said the deal was neutral for Rostelekom in the immediate future. "Everything will depend on who will be the management and what they would like to do with the company long-term."
Troika-Dialog said in an investment note that Rostelekom's performance was likely to suffer as its cash flow would go through Svyazinvest.

Rostelekom shares, which closed on Thursday at $2.50 after the merger plan was aired, were at $2.54 at 1400 GMT, well up from the day's low of $2.38. Telecoms, despite the massive investment needed to update equipment across Russia, have been one of the star sectors among investors in Russia.

Apart from Rostelekom, which has a market share of up to 85 percent in international and long-distance traffic, regional providers in Moscow, St Petersburg and other cities have also attracted investors.
"As long as we have this uncertainty and the possibility of it being handled badly, investors will be restrained. They will be more cautious than previously," said Mellstroem.
However, he said the transfer of shares to Svyazinvest would make modernisation of the sector more coordinated and make it easier to attract a strategic investor.
Troika-Dialog said part of Rostelekom's revenues would be allocated to regional firms through Svyazinvest.
Russia had tried to sell a 25 percent stake in Svyazinvest to a strategic investor. Italy's Stet SpA won a tender last year for the stake but the deal fell through before completion.

"They couldn't sell it because the nature of Svyazinvest is unclear," said United City Bank telecoms anlyst Natalya Ivanova. The link with Rostelekom was aimed at raising Svayzinvest's value, she added.
Krapivin said some investors may swap out of Rostelekom and into Svyazinvest to increase their exposure to regional companies but this would depend on the price.
Interfax news agency on Thursday quoted privatisation minister Alfred Kokh as saying the government could raise $1-2 billion from selling off part of the new company.

But the deal has raised some concern about privatisation policy. The World Bank's chief economist in Moscow, Vladimir Konovalov, said strategic investors could introduce new thinking and increase efficiency in privatising natural monopolies.
"What we are seeing is a process which is well and truly maintaining the control of the existing management of these firms," he said.
